subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF COMPLETION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to address the House today, this seventh day of November, 1985, on the 100th anniversary of the driving of the last spike at Craigellachie, British Columbia.
That historic event, which occurred at 9.22 a.m., was truly one of the most important moments in Canada's history. With the final drive of a hammer, Canada emerged as a united country from coast to coast. A ribbon of steel brought us together as a nation. It gave meaning and substance to the word "Canada". Completion of the transcontinental railway realized our national dream. It serves as a monument and testimony to the spirit, conviction and determination of our forebears.
The sheer act of pushing the iron rail across this land, through muskeg and mountain, over river and plain, stands as a symbol of Canada and the Canadian spirit. That desire to build, to work the vast reaches of Canada, remains a vital element of our national character. The last spike resonates in our imagination and national identity. While it was the end of an epic task, it also marked the beginning of many new and exciting ventures, serving as a springboard for Canada's future.
For the next 100 years, our railways and our transportation system would be instrumental in Canada's economic and social development. The system gave us a base, a link on which to take hold and grow. Now we stand on the verge of a new era in our nation's history. As we look to that future, we again depend on our transportation system to provide the enterprise, innovation and excellence which helped to build our great nation.
Today, just as a century ago, we recognize the importance of transportation to Canada's future and the need to respond with equal vision and spirit to the challenge of building a foundation for national development. To this end, the Government is committed to developing a new legislative framework for transportation to lead us into the 21st century.
Our goal is to develop a transportation system which contributes to the competitiveness of our commerce, a dynamic and energetic system serving new demands. To do so, we must adopt new technology and fresh innovations to provide a wider range of services. We are world leaders in transportation technology, and we must build upon that strength.
We are confident that in a new environment the transportation community will respond to the challenge. Our framework, as outlined in Freedom to Move, encourages the competitive
November 7, 1985

spirit and energy of Canadians to meet our transportation needs.
One hundred years ago, the driving of the last spike helped make our national dream a reality. The spirit of that national dream is alive in Canada today. We are a nation of builders; we take pride in having forged a country out of the rock and soil of our land. The challenges ahead are great; together we can conquer them with the boldness, vision and imagination which made this land a nation.
In conclusion, on this historic day I want to extend sincere congratulations to Canadian Pacific, its management and to all its employees across Canada, whose spirit, dedication and enthusiasm are an inspiration to us all.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF COMPLETION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT

Mr. Speaker, November 7, 1885, was a red letter day in Canada's history, when the CPR train travelled from coast to coast for the first time. Canadian Press reporter David Gersovitz commemorated this event in a very interesting article on the Canadian Pacific.
Ever since Canadian Pacific completed its first transcontinental railroad link, it has played and has continued to play a major role in the economic development of our country. Since that day 100 years ago, Canada's expansion has been impressive. The prosperity we have in this country would certainly not extend to all its regions without the major communication links provided at the beginning of the century by the railroad.
Interestingly, and I quote David Gersovitz;
In Canada, however, this project was essential-
-that is, building a railroad that would connect Canada from coast to coast was absolutely-
-essential to this country's development, something which could not become a reality without a transcontinental railroad link. Those who wanted a united Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific claimed that a railroad line cutting across the entire continent, across the formidable Canadian shield, would keep the West from being swallowed up by the United States.
It is a fact that to develop what we know today as Canada's five main regions, it was necessary to cross that formidable obstacle, the Rocky Mountains, and to reach the Pacific. It is thanks to the pioneer spirit and the enterprise of Canadian Pacific that this dream could become a reality and that Canada is a country stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and since that time, to a third coast, on the Arctic Ocean.
As suggested by the Minister, we should congratulate the administrators of the Canadian Pacific who have diversified their operations over a number of years. This corporation, one of the most important in Canada, is the property of a great many Canadian shareholders.
I want to congratulate both the shareholders, who represent a significant part of the Canadian population, the administra-
Statements by Ministers
tors of the Canadian Pacific for their entrepreneurship, but also and especially the workers, not only those who have built the railway but also those who over the years have directly contributed to the success of that company.
Today being November 7, I cannot help being somewhat sorry when I think of the former employees of the Canadian Pacific who retired before 1978 with a lifetime pass as a result of their years of service for that company. They were used to travel with their lifetime passes which were unilaterally cancelled. I dare hope that, on this 100th Anniversary, the administrators of the Canadian Pacific will demonstrate their kind generosity for their former dedicated employees by announcing within the next few hours or days that they will return to these pensioners the passes which they certainly deserve.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF COMPLETION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a third generation employee of Canadian Pacific Limited-my grandfather having started employment with Canadian Pacific Limited in 1904, followed by my father and then myself-I join with the Minister in his remarks. I only wish the Minister had had more to say.
It is true that this is an historic anniversary. However, there is also an historical record which all Canadians and Members of this House should be reminded of. The workers, the immigrants-who worked, for the most part, under slave-labour conditions-deserve more recognition. One thinks immediately of the Chinese labour involved in the building of the Canadian Pacific railway line. Scores of those workers died in the process. They had to pay a head tax and live like animals, and all for two bits a day. Had it not been for those workers, that line would never have been finished. Recognition has to be given to the contribution of those workers.
So, while this is an historic event, it also is an opportune time to be reminded of this historic behaviour of this corporation, behaviour that represents a century of corporate welfare.
As was said in 1880 or 1881 by the then Leader of the Official Opposition: "Since we are putting up all of this money, land, mineral rights, subsidies, and so forth, why don't we own it?"
And we are still doing it. This particular corporation owes over $1 billion in deferred corporate taxes. It is a corporation that has got out from under commitments and agreements as to the type and amount of service that it would provide forever and a day, not the least of which was the agreement in respect of maintaining a statutory freight rate for the movement of grains.
The CPR has quite a record when it comes to bad corporate citizenship, but the act that takes the cake is the arbitrary cancelling of the passes of its own pensioners.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext:
Last September 19, Mr. Speaker, a very strong earthquake hit Mexico, and we all know the aftermath. According to estimates, 8,000 people died in this tragedy and 30,000 more were injured. Material destruction was widespread-thousands of homes, schools, hospitals. Given the extent of the catastrophy, the international community rallied to provide help.
Mr. Speaker, I think that all Members of the House can be proud of Canada's quick response to this tragedy. Less than 36 hours after the earthquake, the Canadian Government had announced a $1 million contribution for emergency assistance through the Canadian International Development Agency, CIDA. Without delay, we sent to Mexico a cargo of essential equipment along with expert staff. On September 24, we
announced an additional $250,000 contribution to a fund administered by our embassy in Mexico and reserved for small assistance projects. I should think that Canadians who had close relatives or friends in Mexico were also grateful for the exceptional efforts made by Department of External Affairs consular personnel to find people from whom no news had been received and to assist our fellow Canadians who needed help.

Last September, Mr. Speaker, I indicated that the Government would address itself to the matter of providing longer term aid as well. While the film crews are gone from Mexico, our determination to assist those in need remains. It is for the purpose of reporting to the House on that aspect of our work that I wish to speak today.

Our first task was to assess the needs and, to that end, Canada worked in close co-operation with Mexico. As soon as the Mexican Government knew what its priorities were with respect to long-term reconstruction, a Canadian planning mission was sent to Mexico. This team was made up of representatives of two Canadian non-governmental organizations, a spokesman for the business world, and CIDA officials. The members of the mission met with officials of various Mexican Government levels. We also consulted other donor countries, multilateral institutions, private interests and Mexican NGOs.
Mr. Speaker, following these discussions and an assessment of requirements, I am happy to announce that the Government of Canada will be using CIDA budgets to allocate an additional $3,750,000 for aid to Mexico. Areas that will benefit from this assistance-again, further to the discussions we had with the Mexican authorities-are education, housing and health.
The funds will be distributed as follows: first, one million dollars will be spent to rebuild and equip facilities on the campus of the National College for Technical and Professional Training, where a building collapsed, causing numerous casualties among the student population.
Second, I am happy to announce that CIDA will set aside one million dollars for the reconstruction of low-cost housing units and community facilities.
These funds will be channelled through Canadian NGOs under the auspices of the Canadian Council for International Co-operation. The project will be carried out in the most severely stricken communities, in co-operation with Mexican community agencies.
Third, we are allocating the sum of one million dollars for a rural health and pure water project, to be carried out by UNICEF in Guerrero State, which sufferred considerable damage. Beneficiaries of this project will be the peasants in the many isolated communities in this State.
Fourth, a special allocation of $500,000 will be set aside to cope with any additional requests we may receive within these

November 7, 1985

three areas. Finally, an additional $250,000 will be made available to the Canadian Embassy for its small projects program. Experience has shown that this is an ideal way to respond to immediate construction needs.
Yesterday, our embassy's management committee, which met to approve the initial series of projects, was already proceeding to identify specific projects. These will include rebuilding a primary school, a nursery school, a shelter for young girls and a community co-operative for manufacturing bricks.
These new contributions raise the total value of our aid to Mexico for both emergency assistance and long-term reconstruction to $5 million. I might add that this was done in under 50 days.
Canadians have a very special feeling of solidarity for this hospitable country which remains one of their favourite holiday destinations. Once again, Canada has proven to be true to its humanitarian traditions. 1 must say that it is indeed an honour for me to represent it whenever the time comes for assistance to be provided to countries and people in need.

And I want to pay tribute to all those who made it possible for us to act effectively in such difficult circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, the awful tragedy which occured last September 19 certainly hit the consciousness of people throughout the world. While I was naturally impressed by the announcement in today's statement that additional funds will be sent to various agencies to help these people recover from this terrible tragedy, what strikes me most forcibly is the feeling of solidarity and sympathy which has emerged amongst various nations. Immediately following the announcement of this earthquake, independently from any expression of opinion by whatever political regime, there was an immediate feeling in the consciousness of all human beings that they had to do something to help. This always strikes me when such tragedies occur and God knows that there have been a lot of them in the last 20 years: earthquakes, floods, tornadoes, and so on. Of course, I am not speaking about the hunger problem, but about the fact that human beings can suddenly put aside their differences to help a brother or a sister who is suffering and in need of assistance. However, I always ask myself a question: Why is it that we are so quick to provide assistance when such events happen and so quick to forget as soon as the situation is more or less back to normal?
I must tell the Minister that, naturally, there can be no disagreement with her statement. I must also tell her that we would like more to be done. We always want more in such circumstances, which is quite normal.
However, I would like to ask her whether it is truly possible to fool around with the funds provided to our embassies. For
Statements by Ministers
my part, both as member and as chairman of the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, 1 have always urged that additional funds be provided to our embassies which can provide assistance on the spot to those who need it, immediately and at much less cost.
I have made this suggestion throughout the years and I would like the Minister to take note of it and refer it to the Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). First, I would like more and more thought to be given to the possibility of increasing the funds provided not only to nongovernment organizations, because they are directly involved, and often act more quickly than large bureaucratic organizations.
Second, if possible, I would like the funds allocated to embassies, which are directly accountable to the Department, and I am not speaking about the embassies in European countries, because there are virtually no such funds provided for them, but about embassies in underdeveloped or Third World countries, to increase gradually each year so that the ambassador could provide assistance immediately and on the spot after making a single phone call, and even if it is impossible to make such a call.
1 would like the Minister to consider increasing the amount allocated to these funds placed at the disposal of embassies.
I would also like to join the Minister, but I would like to do so in a spectacular way, on behalf not only of this Party but of all Canadians, in order to commend officials of External Affairs who really, this time, outdid themselves . . . one casual look is enough, and it is more eloquent. But the Department deployed itself. . . I would like the Minister to transmit to her Department and to all those people who will be listening to us anyway, our most heartfelt thanks. They really have been at the complete disposal of Canadians.
The External Affairs Department is often criticized by certain people. We are not aware of what those persons have to go through. I for one have great admiration for the Department and its officials who represent us, often in an anonymous way, and when it so happens that one mistake is made, right away the entire department is criticized.
Well then, I have seen them at work, I was there, and Canadians also were able to see that on TV, and it was a very good thing that people could see the work done by Canadians at that time. I want the Minister to know that we are proud of those Canadians who work in her Department. This does not necessarily mean it is because of this Government, of course, and I want the Department to be aware of it. But I want to commend the Minister for any initiatives she may have taken.
On page 2 of her statement, it is said that a planning mission was sent to Mexico. Because of our desire to be well informed about this rather than out of mere curiosity, 1 would appreciate getting the list from her if only to commend those people who work for Canada, and to know who they are. For

November 7, 1985
Statements by Ministers
the future, this could provide us with ideas when we appear before the Committee on Reform . . . the Committee on the green paper, for making suggestions to the Government. Personally, as spokesman for this Party, 1 would like to know the names of the mission members and of the representatives of the various levels of Government in Mexico. I would greatly appreciate having the list. I know this is not very complicated, and that the Minister will be happy to send it to us.
I would also appreciate it if, through her Department, the Minister could tell us who were those people who were consulted, which were the other participating countries. Actually I am especially interested in having this information in order to report to my party how other countries responded to such a disaster . .. Because I would like soon to conclude with very concrete proposals which will somewhat extend beyond the statement and which result from the experience we had over the years and which might help the Government of this country. Therefore, 1 would like to know about those people who have been consulted, and about the multilateral institutions from both the private sector and the non-governmental Mexican organizations.
If this is not asking too much from the Minister, I should like her to tell us with respect to the $1 million earmarked for the reconstruction of low cost housing and community facilities, what she thinks would be their cost price in some countries? It is all very well to say that $1 million will be earmarked for the rebuilding of low cost housing, but how many units? Ten, twenty, thirty or fifty? I think that we would then better understand the thrust of the Canadian contribution, and if it is too low, have Canadians understand that we want to be generous and if we believe in world solidarity we should then be much more generous because this kind of solidarity should always be there since we never know who could be the victim sooner or later.
She stated that there will be a supervisory committee. I would like to know which of those non governmental organizations will control the funds made available to them. I am quite pleased, with an eye on the forthcoming holiday season, on this particular occasion of the Minister's statement to encourage Canadians to make their yearly contribution to UNICEF by buying something from them, since the benefits on the sale of all kinds of items are passed on to that organization. This is a concrete example of what UNICEF can do.
Before concluding, since the Speaker tells me that under the Standing Orders I cannot speak longer than the Minister, some day in committee I would like the Minister to reflect with us on the following fact-if the Speaker would allow me, I will take another 30 seconds-which has been bothering me for years and I mean the fact that we know that on this planet earthquakes do occur. There was an earthquake in North Yemen in January 1983; there were floods in South America
in March 1983. I could go as far back as 1980. We hear almost daily about disasters, earthquakes, flood relief for Argentina, floods in Paraguay. We hear about them constantly. What surprises me is that although all western democracies are constantly on the alert to defend themselves, that large military alliances such as NORAD and NATO have the necessary means and structure to defend their member countries within minutes-I am not blaming the Minister-that when a disaster occurs they spread the news that they will generously fight to defend the rights of suffering human beings, and that they do so in a quite unco-ordinated way. It seems to me that the UNDRO which is the United Nations body responsible for seeking help is not as well organized as we would like it to be, so that when a disaster occurs-we know there will be disasters, even though we do not know where or when they will occur-why is there not more co-ordinated effort on the part of each country when an earthquake hits. We are aware that earthquakes can occur either in rural or urban areas. In urban areas, we know that some buildings will crumble. That we know, Mr. Speaker. And day in and day out, medical teams are sent there. I think, Mr. Speaker, that such a suggestion would be quite proper because we would see how we could be prepared in the future, and how we could draw up, as Canadians are experts in this matter, a new world system for the co-ordination of all people who have something to offer to their brothers and sisters in need as the result of a great tragedy.
In my opinion, it could be a Canadian initiative and if the Minister would consider it, I would be willing to study it with her in committee. This could be a tremendous Canadian project that would show the world that if we are prepared to support military organizations, we are also prepared to show our great generosity and resourcefulness in having some sort of organization, multilateral or whatever which would immediately come to the rescue of human beings who are all our friends.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Minister of State for External Relations (Mrs. Vezina) for providing an advance copy of her statement. Accompanying the statement was CIDA's estimate of damage that was done. Perhaps Hon. Members can get an idea of the magnitude of that damage if we compare it with what was considered to be a major disaster in Canada, the tornado which ripped through the community of Barrie in southern Ontario. I make this comparison with no intent to belittle what happened in Barrie. When tragedy strikes one individual, it is felt very keenly by that individual. When tragedy strikes a community, it affects the whole community in a very serious way. I am not in any way trying to belittle what happened in Canada as much as I am trying to show the magnitude of what happened in Mexico.
In Barrie, 12 people were killed, some 200 homes were destroyed, there were 300 injuries and the total loss to local
November 7, 1985

Petitions
business was estimated at some $27 million. As well, some 100 unemployment insurance claims were filed as a result of the incident. In Mexico, there were some 8,000 people killed, 30,000 people injured, 100,000 left homeless and 150,000 left unemployed. As well, there was extensive damage to schools, hospitals and other public buildings. The announcement of an additional $3.75 million in relief is welcome but it is by no means too much to meet the overwhelming needs that exist in Mexico today. It brings our contribution to both emergency assistance and long-term reconstruction to a total of $5 million.
As the Minister said, the film crews are gone from Mexico and will be responding to some new crisis or excitement in another part of the world. However, the need remains long after world attention has shifted. We know that that is the case as well in Africa. When the attention shifts from the drought in the Sahel, the TV cameras leave but the drought and suffering continue.
Canadians are very generous in sharing when confronted with need. However, like other people in the world, we tend to suffer from compassion fatigue when we are confronted by the same issues over and over again. What is unbelievable when it is seen for the first time on television becomes after awhile simply common.
We must have some way of dealing with the long-term needs after the emotional impact of the immediate crisis has passed. The Canadian International Development Agency is set up to meet that kind of need as is Canada's official Development Aid Program. The problem is that we keep backing away from our commitment to that long-term need.
We originally set a goal of .07 per cent of Gross National Product to meet long-term needs. Elowever, in the early 1980s, we moved the target date of that goal to 1990. At this time last year, we said that we were not going to reach that goal by 1990 and moved the date to 1995. The $5 million we are providing for immediate needs in Mexico comes out of a very restricted CIDA budget. By moving the goal posts we are making it more difficult to respond generously to the immediate as well as long-term needs of Mexico. I urge the Government to take that into consideration. As well, I urge the Government to do what it can with agencies such as the International Monetary Fund to ensure generous treatment of Mexico and other Third World countries which are attempting to reschedule very heavy debt payments. This $5 million we are providing is a drop in the bucket and it will be useless unless we enable those countries to get on their own feet economically.
I want to leave the Government with those two suggestions. We appreciate what has been done in this initial quick response to the immediate crisis in Mexico. We urge the Government to reinstate as a goal the .07 per cent of GNP for ODA by 1990 and do what it can to encourage the IMF and World Bank to reschedule Third World countries' debt.

TABLING OF ANNUAL REPORT OF CANAGREX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with some reluctance, but since the House has spent a great deal of time in the past several years trying to reform the House and make the Members of the House more in control of its processes and more in control of the Crown corporations
Point of Order-Mr. Althouse
and agencies that the House establishes, I want to bring to your attention the law as it relates to the Crown corporation, Canagrex. I refer to Volume IV of the Statutes of Canada, Chapter 152. Section 40.(1) reads:
Canagrex shall, within three months after the termination of each financial year-
That financial year ended in March, 1985.
-make a report to the Minister, in such form as he may direct, on the operations of Canagrex for that financial year.
It goes on in subsection 3 to explain:
The Minister shall cause a copy of the report made to him pursuant to subsection (1) to be laid before Parliament-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: TABLING OF ANNUAL REPORT OF CANAGREX
speechtext: Order, please. Do I understand correctly that the Member is rising on a point of order?

subtopic: TABLING OF ANNUAL REPORT OF CANAGREX
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: TABLING OF ANNUAL REPORT OF CANAGREX
speechtext: The Chair believed that the Member was speaking on debate on Canagrex under Bill C-42. Very well, the Member on a point of order.

subtopic: TABLING OF ANNUAL REPORT OF CANAGREX
speechtext:
Yes, 1 believe you even said "point of order" when I was recognized, Mr. Speaker. The subsection reads:
The Minister shall cause a copy of the report made to him pursuant to subsection (1) to be laid before Parliament on any of the first fifteen days that either House of Parliament is sitting after the report is made to him;
We have, therefore, established that the report should have been made to the Minister three months after March 31. We have established that once that report has been received by the Minister in the form that he wishes, he must-he "shall" it says-present that report to the House within 15 sitting days. 1 submit that those sitting days have long since lapsed. It goes on to say that:
-and every annual report laid before Parliament pursuant to this subsection shall stand referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
The reasoning for that is very clear. That is the immediate opportunity for Members of the House to discuss the annual report and to understand the functions of this Crown corporation.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker, because it is my contention that the Government is attempting, with Bill C-42, to avoid the law, to try to change the law with this particular Bill. It has failed to uphold the existing law. I argue that because the Government has failed to live up to the spirit of openness which the Committee on Parliamentary Reform has been trying to instill in the House for the last five or six years, that this Bill at least be set down. It is out of order. Until such time as the existing laws can be adhered to, we should not be dealing with laws that will simply make what is now illegal legal.

speechtext: I wish to inform the House that, because of the ministerial statements, consideration of Government Orders will be extended by 41 minutes this day. Therefore, Private Members' Hour will begin at 5.41 o'clock p.m. I will recognize the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) on debate.
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a point of order. I had time left in the time allotted to me for questions when the House recessed. Do I not-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, the Member is correct, he had time left, but I saw no one rising on questions or comments.
Well, there were a lot of allegations made by previous speakers and 1 thought surely there would be all kinds of questions on what I had said.
You blew it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Nobody wants to talk to you.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap on debate.
You said the Minister was answering those questions, not you.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to rise in my place today to speak against this piece of legislation. The Government has taken the decision to wind up what is probably one of the most creative, productive and valuable Crown corporations ever. Quite frankly, I remember very clearly, not many months ago, when members of the government Party were in Opposition and stood in their places, both in the House and in Committee, speaking about the value of having a corporation such as Canagrex in place. They had some concerns about various aspects of it, but, by and large, agreed with the principle. As a matter of fact, I believe it was the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) who at one time stood in his place and indicated the value of having a Crown corporation such as Canagrex in place. It is peculiar how one forgets about commitments made to various groups once one is in Government. In this case, the group is the farmers of Canada.
When talking about Canagrex, one cannot help but think of corporations such as the Export Development Corporation. It does an effective job in terms of assisting the industrial sector to develop an export option for its products. It has a budget of some $20 million of contingent liability. It provides specific financial lending and insurance assistance to help reduce the very substantial risk in the export of Canadian industrial products overseas. We consider this corporation as an important aspect of our trade policy and an important component of the development of Canada's economy for export trade.
There is also the Canada Commercial Corporation which assists Canadian corporations, both large and small, to find opportunities for expanding the sale of their goods overseas in foreign markets. I believe the record would show that the EDC and the CCC have very impressive track records and could in fact accomplish much more.

November 7, 1985

However, there is no commitment to our farmers. They take advantage of our most important resource, agriculture, in order to grow foodstuffs for domestic purposes as well as for sale overseas. There is no commitment to assist the development of those overseas trade opportunities. Canagrex was a Crown corporation that was attempting to do just that. Although it had not been given enough time to prove itself, it had a reasonable track record in the short time it operated since its establishment in January, 1984. Canagrex had a reasonable track record and had made a great many sales. It provided many opportunities for individuals and firms throughout the country. I ask Hon. Members to stand in their place and deny that there were not literally dozens of sales which had not taken place prior to the formation of Canagrex and that there were many more potential sales before the Government decided to wind down its operations.
The Government has taken this action strictly for political reasons. It was fashionable during the campaign to denounce and decry all Crown corporations and say that Government involvement in such enterprises was bad. When one considers the rhetoric used about Canagrex, it was very disappointing that people would politicize the development of this newly formed Crown corporation. As a result of that rhetoric and the attacks made against Canagrex by the Conservatives during the election campaign, I suggest they felt an obligation to wind it down once they formed the Government.
I believe we should comment on the various aspects of Canagrex itself. In fact, Canagrex was a model of what Crown corporations should be in the future. There was a requirement to review its effectiveness every five years. Another section in the Canagrex Act enabled the Auditor General to have access to its books at any time and to have full access to its operations so that the people of Canada would know if they were getting their money's worth.
Canagrex consisted of a broadly based Board of Directors that reflected the need for wide ranging representation. The Chief Executive Officer and President, Mr. Edwin Story, had acquired extensive experience in the export field over a long period of time. He knew the export field and knew what was required in terms of opening new market opportunities. Mr. Glenn Flaten was Chairman of the 11 member Board of Directors for Canagrex. He was President of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and a member of numerous other agricultural related associations and boards. Mr. Howard Malcolm was President of the Canadian Pork Council and obviously familiar with the hog industry. Mr. Walter Kroeker was President and Director of Vegetable Growers in Manitoba, a vegetable farmer and businessman, and past-President of the Canadian Horticultural Council. There were many qualified individuals on the board who represented various sectors of the agricultural industry. They played an active role once Canagrex began operations in January, 1984. It was most unfortunate that there was no consultation between the Government and those involved in the agricultural community before the decision was made to wind down this operation, especially when one considers that the Government promised
Canagrex Dissolution Act
to conduct a great deal of consultations with groups before making decisions. That was not the case here.
Many people sent telegrams, wrote letters and sent delegations to Ottawa, at the eleventh hour, once they heard that the Government was planning to wind down the affairs of Canagrex. Let me refer to some of those telegrams. A telegram from Mary Boyd of Charlottetown states:
Please reconsider Canagrex Bill. Should be discussed by Agricultural Committee. Canada needs Canagrex.
Another telegram from a farmer on Prince Edward Island requests the Government to reconsider the Canagrex decision. He asks that the Canagrex officials appear before the Agriculture Committee to explain the work of the Crown Corporation. Robert Jeppsen of New Brunswick, who was with the National Farmers' Union states:
Let me state my disappointment with the cancellation of Canagrex. Our present system of exporting potatoes has not proven beneficial to potato producers nor have our exporters been responsible agents abroad. We see Canagrex as a sign of hope. Therefore we request your Government to reconsider Canagrex and bring it to the Standing Committee on Agriculture for hearings.
A dairy farmer from Grand Falls, New Brunswick and another farmer from Manitoba have indicated how vital Canagrex was to the farm communities and their future. There are pages and pages containing the names of active and knowledgeable farmers who realize the potential of that sector. That potential will disappear because of Conservative rhetoric and ideological commitment about Crown corporations.
My hon. friend, the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) indicated that we are concerned about proceeding with this Bill because it appears that it is against the law. For example, Section 40(1) of the Canagrex Act states:
Canagrex shall, within three months after the termination of each financial year, make a report to the Minister, in such form as he may direct, on the operations of Canagrex for that financial year.
That is straightforward. It goes on:
(3) The Minister shall cause a copy of the report made to him pursuant to subsection (1) to be laid before Parliament on any of the first fifteen days that either House of Parliament is sitting after the report is made to him; and every annual report laid before Parliament pursuant to this subjection shall stand referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
It is our interpretation, as New Democrats, that Government is proceeding in an inappropriate manner. It has not fulfilled its legal obligations. We feel very uncomfortable dealing with something by which the Government is breaking the law, as best as we can determine.
Therefore, in light of our hesitancy to proceed with something that may in fact be illegal, and considering that we have many pressing matters to deal with that are of a legal nature, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That this House do now adjourn.
